newsitem.title: USA: South Korea agrees to recall spy-case diplomat.
newsitem.headline: South Korea agrees to recall spy-case diplomat.

text.p: South Korea has agreed to recall a Washington embassy official identified as being involved in a spy operation, the State Department said on Thursday.

"The Korean Foreign Ministry indicates that they are recalling Captain (Dong il-) Baek," deputy spokesman Glyn Davies told reporters. "Captain Baek has been instructed to return to Seoul by the Korean government."

The FBI announced on Wednesday that Robert Kim, a Korean-born civilian computer specialist for a U.S. Navy intelligence agency, had been arrested on espionage charges for passing secret and top-secret documents to Baek, a naval attache at the South Korean embassy in Washington.
Davies said the United States considered the recall of Baek a cooperative gesture on the part of its "strong ally" South Korea but added that more is expected.
"It does not finally resolve this issue," he said. "So we look to further discussions with the Korean government on this issue. We want them to cooperate as we go forward in this investigation."

He said the United States was "looking for all the information we can get" both to prosecute Kim and to assess what damage may have been done to U.S. intelligence interests. He said South Korean officials understood "what is expected of them at this stage."

In announcing the arrest of Kim on Wednesday, the FBI described him as a 56-year-old government employee for the past 18 years, who worked at a U.S. Navy intelligence office in Suitland, Maryland, near Washington.
It said he was arrested without incident on Tuesday night at a diplomatic reception at Fort Myer, Virginia.
Kim was charged with passing classified information to a South Korean agent -- Baek, a naval officer who arrived in the United States in 1994.

At a five-minute court hearing in Alexandria, Virginia, on Wednesday, prosecutor Robert Chestnut said Kim should be held in jail without bail "because of his close relationship with Korea, there is a serious risk of flight."

Jim Clark, a court-appointed defence lawyer, replied that Kim's wife and son live in the area and denying him bond "unfairly prejudges Mr. Kim." A federal magistrate set a new hearing for Monday on whether Kim should be held without bond.
Kim, of Sterling, Virginia, was born in Seoul and became a U.S. citizen in 1974. He was charged with passing the classified information from May through September.
FBI agent Gloria Harbold said in an affidavit that Kim regularly searched the Navy intelligence computer system for secret and top-secret documents.
"Kim copies and stores these documents in his work computer, removes classification markings and prints them on his office printer and transmits them to Baek," she said.
Harbold said Kim had stored in his computer a number of "K" files containing U.S. government documents on North and South Korea and other Asian-Pacific countries.

A Justice Department official said the case was much less signficant than the scandal involving former Central Intelligence Agency agent Aldrich Ames, who was sentenced to life in prison for spying for Moscow for $2.5 million.
Kim was charged under an espionage law that carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison, the official said.
